# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–21 (Complete – Updated 149)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Spring of sixth year** (Chapter 21). Winter of fifth year (Chapter 20) complete with Christmas at Queen's Crawley, Pitt's parliamentary debut, and Amelia's maternal sacrifice. **Chapter 20 events (Autumn through Spring)**: Sir Pitt (elder) dies summer 1816; Pitt becomes Baronet and MP; Miss Crawley dies spring 1816; house renovation November through winter on Great Gaunt Street (black brick removed, bronze knocker gilded, railings painted); Christmas gathering at Queen's Crawley; return to London with house ready for Pitt's family; Parliament session begins with Pitt establishing himself as profound dissembler hiding ambitions to rise among party chiefs.
- **Locations**: (As before, plus) Salwick (harbor town; Lutho Hollmere location in Chapter 21).
- **Parliamentary and financial context (Chapter 20)**: Pitt attends first session assiduously, learns House routine thoroughly, presents petition from Mudbury, makes acquaintance with ministers and party chiefs, determines to rank among them before many years pass.

## Main Characters

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley) (Chapters 19-20)**
- **Manipulation and cultivation of Pitt**: November visit demonstrates Rebecca's strategic warmth—greets Pitt alone at hotel, invites him to Curzon Street; her hospitalities irresistible through artless frank manner. Cooks salmi of Lord Steyne's pheasants, serves wine from Steyne's cellars (falsely claiming Rawdon obtained it cheaply from France), listens with "tenderest kindly interest" while hemming shirt for little Rawdon, sings and coaxes him. On departure, kisses hand from carriage; performance moves Pitt emotionally—broods that she "respected him," that Rawdon is "foolish dull fellow," that Lady Jane is "mum and stupid" compared to "brilliant little Becky." Rebecca delicately hinted all comparisons herself.
- **Financial manipulation and authority**: Accepted small sum for little Rawdon's benefit via Pitt's check. Given full orders by Pitt to sell, barter, confiscate, or purchase furniture for house renovation; oversees Miss Briggs and little Rawdon superintending female band stitching blinds and hangings.
- **Credit through Lord Steyne's appearance**: Sight of Marquis of Steyne's carriage-lamps at her door at midnight kept creditor faith; suggests creditors extend credit believing her Steyne's mistress. Described as "guiltless very likely" yet "writhing and pushing onward towards what they call 'a position in society.'"
- **Contempt for Lady Jane and psychological warfare**: Profound dissembler hiding scorn for Lady Jane's "sweetness and kindness," finding her goodness "annoying." When Lady Jane tells stories to children, Rebecca enters sneering with "green scornful eyes"; poor Lady Jane grows silent under "baleful glances"; her "simple little fancies shrank away tremulously, as fairies in the story-books, before a superior bad angel." Rebecca caricatures Court suit, shows sketch to Lord Steyne who carries it off delighted; tells Steyne she has "no taste for bread and butter" when caricaturing Lady Jane. Rebecca and Lady Jane do not see much of each other except when younger brother's wife, having object to gain, frequents her; they "my-loved and my-deared each other assiduously, but kept apart generally."
- **Court presentation and Lord Steyne's patronage**: Lord Steyne met Pitt at Becky's house, impressed by Rebecca's ease, sprightliness, delight with which other men listened to her. Made no doubt Pitt commenced career in public life; as neighbours, left calling card within day or two, never having thought fit to notice predecessor.
- **Maternal rejection**: Would have preferred to leave little Rawdon behind at Christmas but for Lady Jane's urgent invitations and Rawdon's "symptoms of revolt and discontent" at her neglect of son.

**Sir Pitt Crawley (younger) – Baronet, MP (Chapters 19-20)**
- **Parliamentary ambition**: First session as profound dissembler hiding projects; presents petition from Mudbury only; attends assiduously, learns House routine and business thoroughly. At home peruses Blue Books to alarm of Lady Jane, who fears he kills himself by late hours. Makes acquaintance with ministers and party chiefs, determining to rank among them before many years pass. Displays complacency examining his thin Court suit legs, thinking himself "killing."
- **November visit and emotional response**: Comes to town November to see lawyers; lodges nearly week with Rawdon and Rebecca at Curzon Street. Appreciates Rebecca's salmi and wine from Steyne's cellars. Each day returns from Gray's Inn lawyers to Curzon Street's blazing fire with increasing gladness; feels "quite a pang at departing" when leaving. Broods that Rebecca respected him, that Rawdon is "foolish dull fellow," that Lady Jane is "mum and stupid" compared to "brilliant little Becky."
- **Financial circumstances and continued concealment**: Knows brother's family has nothing to live upon; aware he appropriated money that ought to have fallen to younger brother; feels "secret pangs of remorse." When Rebecca delicately obtained money for Rawdon's creditors, Pitt grew alarmed and launched long explanation of his own straitened circumstances: tenants won't pay, father's expenses involved him, wants to pay off incumbrances, bankers and agents overdrawn. Made compromise with Rebecca, giving small sum for little Rawdon's benefit. **Christmas generosity**: Before Christmas ends, screwed up courage to give brother another draft on bankers for hundred pounds—act causing him "cruel pangs at first" but making him "glow afterwards to think himself one of the most generous of men." Encourages Jim of Rectory to pay addresses to young lady with understanding he shall be presented to living when vacated.
- **At Christmas dinner**: Sits at head of table with Rebecca at right hand, uncommonly attentive to sister-in-law; perches Rawdon Junior on high chair by his side after dinner; reads prayers from great gilt book with domestics.

**Colonel Rawdon Crawley (Chapter 20)**
- **Increasing isolation and subjugation**: Feels himself more and more isolated every day amid Rebecca's intrigues. Allowed to go to club more; to dine abroad with bachelor friends; to come and go when liked, without questions asked. Sits for hours in brother's house very silent, thinking, doing little as possible. Glad to be employed on errand. "Beat and cowed into laziness and submission." Delilah (Rebecca) imprisoned him, cut his hair off. "Bold and reckless young blood of ten-years back was subjugated and was turned into a torpid, submissive, middle-aged, stout gentleman."
- **Concern for son and family**: Strong attachment to little Rawdon; manifests "symptoms of revolt and discontent" at Rebecca's neglect of boy. Tells Rebecca reproachfully, "He's the finest boy in England... and you don't seem to care for him, Becky, as much as you do for your spaniel." **Christmas activities**: Wraps little Rawdon in shawls and comforters; hoists child onto roof of coach at White Horse Cellar; answers all boy's questions connected with road. Walks and rides with brother Pitt examining improvements, discussing estate matters. Departs with "utmost heaviness of heart" after Christmas.

**Little Rawdon (Son) (Chapters 19-20)**
- **Physical description**: Fine open-faced boy with blue eyes and waving flaxen hair; sturdy in limb; generous and soft in heart; about eight years old.
- **Christmas journey and activities**: Rides on coach roof with father at White Horse Cellar at dawn; journey "of infinite pleasure"; father answers all questions. At Hall, enters "perfect palace of enchantment and wonder" with galleries, ancient bedrooms, pictures, china, armour. Takes command of small party with Pitt Binkie and Matilda; they follow him with "great reverence"; his happiness and pleasure in country "extreme." Fox-hunt spectacle famous sight for little Rawdon; remains on doorsteps after hunt departs—"wondering and happy." Departs with "utmost heaviness of heart."

**Amelia Osborne (Mrs. George Osborne) (Chapter 20)**
- **Refusal of Osborne's offer and maternal integrity**: When Mr. Osborne formally offers to make little George heir to fortune and provide Amelia allowance, conditioned on child living entirely with grandfather with only occasional permitted visits, Amelia responds with rare anger. Tears letter into hundred fragments, declares "I marry again! I take money to part from my child! Who dares insult me by proposing such a thing?" Calls proposal cowardly; refuses answer; bows attorney (Mr. Poe) out like tragedy Queen. Never tells parents of Osborne's letter or interview.
- **Maternal sacrifice and Christmas determination (Chapter 20)**: As Sedley household falls into financial ruin, Amelia prioritizes son's welfare above all. Sacrifices personal purse to keep son in health. When promised Christmas clothes must be countermanded, Amelia breaks matter to Georgy who makes "loud outcry—'Everybody had new clothes at Christmas. The others would laugh at him.'" Despite poverty, Amelia remembers India shawl sent by Dobbin; walks to Ludgate Hill India shop flushed and eager; merchant gives twenty guineas. Purchases Parents' Assistant and Sandford and Merton Georgy longed for; writes in fly-leaf "George Osborne, A Christmas gift from his affectionate mother." Books extant to this day with fair delicate superscription.
- **Crisis of conscience (Chapter 20 – NEW)**: After her mother's anguished outburst ("Books, when the whole house wants bread! Books, when to keep you and your son in luxury... I've sold every trinket I had, the India shawl from my back even down to the very spoons"), Amelia surrenders all remaining money to mother in trembling silence. Retreats to room and "sank down in despair and utter misery." Sees now that "her selfishness was sacrificing the boy." Realizes "But for her he might have wealth, station, education, and his father's place, which the elder George had forfeited for her sake. She had but to speak the words, and her father was restored to competency and the boy raised to fortune." This conviction strikes her "tender and stricken heart" with terrible force. **Mrs. Sedley's reproach**: In hysterical outburst, accuses Amelia of breaking her heart with books and the boy "whom you are ruining, though part with him you will not." Contrasts Amelia's refusal with Jos's desertion of father in old age, and George's potential to be "provided for, and who might be rich" while "my dear, dear old man is without a sh--shilling." Speech echoes through small house where other female inmates hear entire colloquy.

**The Marquis of Gaunt and His Family (Chapter 20 – NEW, background)**
- **Lord Gaunt's properties (Chapter 20 – NEW)**: Besides town palace, possesses Castle Strongbow with woods on Shannon shore; Gaunt Castle in Carmarthenshire where Richard II was taken prisoner; Gauntly Hall in Yorkshire with two hundred silver teapots for breakfast of guests; Stillbrook in Hampshire, described as "humble place of residence" (farm) with wonderful furniture later sold at lord's demise.
- **Lord Gaunt married Lady Blanche Thistlewood** (daughter of Bareacres house). A wing of Gaunt House assigned to this couple; head of family chose to govern and reign supreme while son lived little at home, disagreed with wife, borrowed upon post-obits beyond moderate sums allowed by father. Marquis knew every shilling of son's debts; at demise found himself possessor of many heir's bonds, purchased for their benefit, devised to children of younger son.
- **Lady Gaunt had no children**, causing Lord Gaunt's dismay and natural enemy father's "chuckling delight."
- **Lord George Gaunt (Marquis's younger son)** (Chapter 20 – NEW): Desired to return from Vienna (where engaged in "waltzing and diplomacy") and contract matrimonial alliance with Honourable Joan, only daughter of John Johnes, First Baron Helvellyn, head of banking firm Jones, Brown, and Robinson, Threadneedle Street. From this union sprang several sons and daughters whose doings do not appertain to this story.
- **Lord George Gaunt's diplomatic career and mental breakdown (Chapter 20 – NEW)**: Marriage "at first was a happy and prosperous one." Lord George could not only read but write pretty correctly; spoke French with considerable fluency; was one of finest waltzers in Europe. With these talents and interest at home, little doubt he would rise to highest dignities in profession. Wife felt courts were her sphere; her wealth enabled splendid receptions in continental towns. Talk of appointing him minister; bets laid at Travellers' he would be ambassador ere long. **Sudden behavioral crisis**: Secretary's extraordinary behaviour erupted—at grand diplomatic dinner given by his chief, he started up and declared pate de foie gras poisoned. Went to ball at Bavarian envoy (Count de Springbock-Hohenlaufen) hotel with head shaved, dressed as Capuchin friar. "Not a masked ball"—something queer, people whispered. "His grandfather was so. It was in the family." **Forced withdrawal and concealment**: Wife and family returned to England; took up abode at Gaunt House. Lord George gave up post on European continent, was gazetted to Brazil. "But people knew better; he never returned from that Brazil expedition—never died there—never lived there—never was there at all. He was nowhere; he was gone out altogether." Gossips: "Brazil is St. John's Wood. Rio de Janeiro is a cottage surrounded by four walls, and George Gaunt is accredited to a keeper, who has invested him with the order of the Strait-Waistcoat." (Claim: institutionalized, likely for mental illness.)

**Narrator's commentary (Chapter 20 – NEW)**: States Lady Gaunt "in her high station, had to submit to many a private indignity and to hide many secret griefs under a calm face." Invites readers to "console ourselves by thinking comfortably how miserable our betters may be, and that Damocles, who sits on satin cushions and is served on gold plate, has an awful sword hanging over his head in the shape of a bailiff, or an hereditary disease, or a family secret, which peeps out every now and then from the embroidered arras in a ghastly manner, and will be sure to drop one day or the other in the right place."

**Tom Eaves (Chapter 20 – NEW)**: Society gossip who expounds on elder brothers' feelings toward younger sons. Claims "every elder brother looks upon the cadets of the house as his natural enemies, who deprive him of so much ready money which ought to be his by right." Cites George Mac Turk, Lord Bajazet's eldest son, who claims if he had will upon coming to title, would "clear the estate by chopping off all his younger brothers' heads at once; and so the case is, more or less, with them all." Declares "they are all Turks in their hearts." Notes that having "laid out every shilling of his fortune on an annuity, Tom could afford to bear no malice to his nephews and nieces, and to have no other feeling with regard to his betters but a constant and generous desire to dine with them." Character reveals through obsequious behaviour—hat drops off when great man approaches, rushes forward with bow and grin showing he knows the world "in the Tomeavesian way."

**Minor Characters (Chapter 20)**
- **Mr. Osborne**: After Jane tells him she saw his grandson, shows no anger but kindly voice. Within fortnight, meditated on matter and made inquiries of Dobbin family regarding her visit. Formally offers to make George heir, provide Amelia allowance, permit occasional visits only.
- **Old Mr. Sedley**: Dabbles in speculation despite Mr. Clapp's remonstrances; never tells how far engaged; wine and coal companies failed; bills fall into arrear; remittances from India not arrived; keeps notion shares must rise.
- **Mrs. Sedley**: Growing infirm and shaken; remains silent or weeps a great deal with Mrs. Clapp in kitchen. In Chapter 20, makes hysterical outburst against Amelia's prioritization of books over household needs.
- **Mr. Clapp**: Former servant of old Sedley; after master's disaster, found other employment quickly; remains faithfully attached; remonstrates against Sedley's speculations.
- **Breena** (Character 20 – NEW): Went along to live in Harrowgate.
- **Lutho Hollmere** (Character 21 – NEW, fragmentary): Resident of harbor town Salwick; "complained of an aching back, as usual" (spring of sixth year, Chapter 21). Narrative function remains unclear; isolated from main Crawley-Osborne plot.

## Critical Facts
- **Osborne's financial coercion versus Amelia's maternal integrity**: Mr. Osborne attempts to purchase custody through allowance conditioned on separation. Amelia's refusal demonstrates maternal love transcends financial security; she prefers poverty with son. However, her mother's anguished reproach plants seeds of terrible doubt—recognition that her refusal may indeed be ruining the boy's prospects and her father's financial security through her "selfishness."
- **Sedley family financial collapse complete**: Bills in arrear; remittances from India not arrived; speculation failed; household in ruin. Amelia has sacrificed all personal money; mother has sold every possession to maintain household and rent payments. Household tension acute; Mrs. Sedley's anguish public and audible throughout house.
- **Rebecca's psychological and financial dominance of Pitt continues**: Campaign of contempt and strategic sabotage of Lady Jane threatens marriage stability. Rebecca cultivates Pitt's emotional dependency through false warmth and flattery; Pitt broods on comparisons between wife and sister-in-law, feels moved by Rebecca's "respect" for him.
- **Rawdon's complete subjugation**: Transformed from "bold and reckless young blood" into "torpid, submissive, middle-aged, stout gentleman" through Rebecca's control. Only emotional anchor remains his son.
- **Hereditary mental illness in Gaunt family**: Lord George Gaunt's public breakdown during diplomatic service (bizarre declarations, inappropriate behaviour, mental derangement) suggests familial predisposition ("His grandfather was so. It was in the family"). Now institutionalized/confined under guise of Brazilian posting.
